# The Span

The rains came early that year and turned the shallow ditch beside the colony into a river.

For the ants of the Cedar Root nest, the ditch had always been a small thing. You climbed down one side, crossed the cracked mud floor, and climbed up the other side to the clover fields, where the aphids kept their sweet herds. Now brown water ran through it, fast and cold, and the clover fields might as well have been on the moon.

The foragers gathered at the edge. Some had tried to swim the first morning. None had come back.

Tessa was a young worker, still pale from the brood chambers, and she wasn't supposed to have opinions. But she had watched the water for two days, and she had noticed something: a single fallen pine needle had lodged across the narrowest part of the stream, one end on each bank. A beetle had walked across it that morning as if nothing were wrong.

"We need a needle," she told the eldest forager, a scarred old ant named Brannoch.

"There are no more needles that long," Brannoch said. "That one was luck."

Tessa looked at the needle, then at the hundreds of ants crowded along the bank, then at her own six legs gripping the mud.

"Then we'll be the needle," she said.

It didn't work the first time. Tessa locked her mandibles around a root at the edge and told the ant behind her to hold onto her back legs, and the next to hold onto that one. The chain stretched out over the water four ants long. Then the current caught the fifth and swept them all sideways in a tangle. Brannoch hauled them back by their legs, coughing and furious.

"You'll drown the whole colony," he said.

"We learned something, though," Tessa said, shaking water from her antennae. "We were too thin. One ant can't hold against the pull. We need to be wide."

So they tried again the next morning. This time the chain was three ants across, each one gripping her neighbors on the left and right as well as the one in front. They didn't build straight out over the water. They angled into the current the way the pine needle had settled, slanted, so the water pushed them toward the far bank instead of away from it.

It took all morning. Ants trembled. Some lost their grip and had to be pulled back up by the others. But the living bridge grew a body length at a time, until at last the ant at the front stretched out one foreleg and touched the opposite bank.

A ripple ran back through the bridge, from ant to ant, faster than words: *Holding. Holding. Holding.*

Then the foragers walked across.

They crossed carefully at first, stepping on their sisters' backs, and then quickly, in a steady dark line. They came back heavy with honeydew and crossed again. By evening the bridge ants were relieved by fresh ones, and those by more.

The rain lasted eleven days, and the bridge stood every one of them.

Long after the ditch dried, the colony kept the knowledge. Young workers practiced linking on twigs and puddles while the old ones watched and corrected their grips. Brannoch, who had called it impossible, became its strictest teacher.

"Wide, not long," he would say. "Lean into the current. And never let go of the one beside you."

Tessa grew old and scarred herself. Each time the rains returned, she went to the water's edge and gripped the first root.
